what_it_does: LLM training and inference move enormous amounts of data — weights (the model's learned parameters), activations (intermediate results during a forward pass), gradients (the error signals used during training), and the KV cache (the running scratchpad of context) — between memory and compute, and this data movement is increasingly the main speed and energy bottleneck. LLM.265 proposes reusing the video encoder and decoder chips that already exist inside modern GPUs (built for compressing H.265/HEVC video) as general-purpose compressors for these LLM tensors (multi-dimensional arrays of numbers). The insight is that LLM tensors have structure similar to video frames: model weights change slowly and smoothly across their dimensions (like a slowly panning camera), activation values repeat patterns across time steps (like consecutive video frames), and KV cache vectors are often correlated with each other. Standard video codec stages — predicting a frame from previous frames, transforming blocks via a math operation called the Discrete Cosine Transform (which concentrates energy into a few large coefficients), then quantizing and entropy-coding the small residuals — can therefore compress LLM tensors meaningfully. The paper claims this requires only modest additions to the existing video hardware, reusing most of the chip area already present.
